periodthree Mamba
periodthree Canto I
periodthree I.
periodthree The day declined, the sun had set,
periodthree For orb and ocean more than met;
periodthree And forth from boughs that heav'nward sprang
periodthree Grotesque and mocking laughter rang.
periodthree Grim scaur and scalp, and mountain side,
periodthree To laughing hill and vale replied;
periodthree The distant wood that fring'd the plain
periodthree With fainter echoes laughed again;
periodthree And cool night-breeze that stirred the reeds,
periodthree And all the dancing water-weeds,
periodthree Bore softer sounds; and on the tide
periodthree The giant halcyon's laughter died.
periodthree II.
periodthree This night twelve moons had passed away
periodthree Seven times, since 'neath the parting ray
periodthree That kissed the murmuring river's breast,
periodthree Young Mamba's mother found her rest.
periodthree She died, but dying left a life
periodthree In pledge for her's amid the strife
periodthree [2] That closes days and opens years,
periodthree With all their future hopes and fears.
periodthree But Mamba's father ne'er was known,
periodthree And no man claimed him for his own.
periodthree Seven summer suns had clothed his head
periodthree With darkly clustering curls, that shed
periodthree A softness o'er the beaming face,
periodthree That bore of pride an early trace.
periodthree Young Borote, who for these short years
periodthree Had kept the pledge that came in tears,
periodthree Nursed with a mourning mother's care
periodthree The offspring of another fair,
periodthree And saw in every grace it wore
periodthree The semblance of one lost before;
periodthree And thus the childless found a child,
periodthree A mother on the orphan smiled,
periodthree And buried babe and mother fond
periodthree Faded in mist the world beyond.
periodthree Thus ever may the ending be
periodthree When our last sun sets gloomily
periodthree And some yet brighter image spring
periodthree From out our dust, that bard may sing,
periodthree Whose deeds shall fire the group around,
periodthree As ears entranced drink in the sound.
periodthree *  *  * * *
periodthree III.
periodthree Her warmest robe became his nest,
periodthree He slept upon her heaving breast,
periodthree Or lay beside the little fire,
periodthree Nor never dreamt he lacked a sire.
periodthree 'Twas thus at eve, and so at night
periodthree When flames made dark young eyes grow bright;
periodthree And when at dawn she rose in bliss
periodthree To wake him with a fondling kiss - 
periodthree Oh! who could paint the tender joy
periodthree Of Borote, as she clasp'd the boy,
periodthree [3] Impetuous pressing 'gainst her breast,
periodthree At once caressing and caress'd?
periodthree She gazed into his eyes, and there,
periodthree Two Borotes bright, a mirror'd pair,
periodthree Smiled from each dark delicious well
periodthree O'er which the silken eyelash fell - 
periodthree Two pictured loves in love enshrined
periodthree Before the portal of the mind.
periodthree IV.
periodthree She bore him to the river banks,
periodthree Where, 'mid the rushes, swaying ranks,
periodthree Lay Nerinella's long canoe
periodthree Floating, impearl'd with glist'ning dew;
periodthree And where the weed of green and red
periodthree It's floating carpet gaily spread,
periodthree Whereon the emerald frog reclined
periodthree Fanned by the fragrance of the wind;
periodthree And all was darkened by the shade
periodthree The water-weeping branches made,
periodthree Save where a paler, tend'rer green
periodthree Made bright the beauty of the scene.
periodthree The morn was gay ere yet the sun
periodthree His heav'nward journey had begun;
periodthree And flow'rs their spicy odours shed
periodthree From drooping branches over-head,
periodthree Whilst those around his tender feet
periodthree Smiled upward from their grassy seat.
periodthree The birds flashed down to drink or lave,
periodthree With varied note and joyous stave,
periodthree And plunging sidelong from the reeds.
periodthree That waver'd 'mid the water-weeds,
periodthree Plashed in the stream so cool and calm,
periodthree O'erhung by many a fern-tree palm;
periodthree And bell-bird peals, whose silvery chimes
periodthree Found in the rippled water rhymes,
periodthree [4] Throughout the perfumed thicket rang,
periodthree Whence the tall-headed bulrush sprang.
periodthree The waking river's dimpled face
periodthree Bore on its waning smile the trace
periodthree Where bird had kissed the brimming tide,
periodthree That tiptoe with its lip replied.
periodthree She paused. Her robe she cast aside,
periodthree And stood in all her naked pride,
periodthree With youthful limbs and queenly grace,
periodthree And more a girl's than woman's face.
periodthree The glorious braids of raven black,
periodthree That rippled down her hollow back - 
periodthree The planted foot - the bosom large,
periodthree That heaved and fell like river marge - 
periodthree And all her fair proportions round,
periodthree Some sisters in the water found:
periodthree 'Twas thus she seem'd, 'twas thus she stood,
periodthree In all her beauty, by the flood.
periodthree *  *  * * *
periodthree V.
periodthree Taking young Mamba by the hand,
periodthree She led him to a pebbly strand;
periodthree And raising up, with gentle might,
periodthree The boy, who danced with wild delight,
periodthree She flung him flying from the brink,
periodthree And watched the wayward urchin sink.
periodthree The waters closed - the circles flew,
periodthree With widening stretch, the shore to woo,
periodthree And foam and bursting bells of light
periodthree Rose from the depths with bubbles bright,
periodthree And soon the reappearing head
periodthree Sprang up, and little palms outspread;
periodthree Then, flinging wide her rounded arms,

periodthree And tossing back the raven hair
periodthree That hid her shapely temples fair,
periodthree [5] Allured the gently-swimming boy,
periodthree Who cleaved the wave with cries of joy.
periodthree VI.
periodthree The boy, with mischief-loving eye,

periodthree And many a patch of bubbling foam

periodthree VII.
periodthree Borote the gentle one - the fair - 
periodthree Stood in her brightness waiting there;

periodthree Thus through the perfumed air they pass'd,

periodthree VIII.
periodthree Young Mamba with the early day
periodthree Arose, and joined his peers at play;

periodthree IX.
periodthree And Mamba ever would beguile
periodthree The time with mirth-provoking smile,
periodthree And tale that brought to Borote bliss.
periodthree One I remember; it was this:-
periodthree Two birds were fighting furiously
periodthree A bird looked down and laughed to see.
periodthree I threw, but missed the fighting pair;
periodthree Then he looked down and laughed at me.
periodthree For this I took a steadier aim,
periodthree And hurled in stick at higher game.
periodthree He wildly laughed, and quivering fell - 
periodthree 'Twas his last laugh - I laughed as well."
periodthree Short were the tales, and soft the clime - 
periodthree The summer in its early prime;
periodthree [8] So passed the days, so fled the hours,
periodthree Amid the wealth of birds and flowers.
periodthree But Mamba could not always be
periodthree A child among the children. He - 
periodthree Fired with the stories of the chase,
periodthree That lent new brightness to his face - 
periodthree Resolved, Nernepten-like, to stand
periodthree A hero-hunter 'mid the band.
periodthree X.
periodthree Nernepten was a warrior bold,
periodthree Though grey of head yet scarcely old,
periodthree Who bore from all the palm away
periodthree In fishing, chase, in fight or fray.
periodthree He lived apart - a silent man,
periodthree A worker - wonder of the clan;
periodthree And brave must that bold spirit be
periodthree That dared to keep him company.
periodthree The old he loved - his ready spear
periodthree Oft furnish'd forth their festive cheer;
periodthree But for the well-grown stalwart ones,
periodthree He looked on these as younger sons,
periodthree And bade them exercise in chase
periodthree By his example in the race.
periodthree From blatant youth he turned away,
periodthree Finding but folly in their say;
periodthree But take to him the bright-eyed child,
periodthree You found him as a woman mild.
periodthree There were no scions of his stock;
periodthree He stood alone - a towering rock,
periodthree O'ershadowing with his mightiness
periodthree The weak ones in life's wilderness.
periodthree XI.
periodthree Nernepten, naked to the waist,
periodthree Sate 'mid the wood himself had placed
periodthree [9] That angled portion, soon to be
periodthree A wangiem whirling rapidly.
periodthree Stripped of its bark, the ruddy pride
periodthree Blushed deeply through the wounded side,
periodthree And painted, with prophetic might,
periodthree Blood to be spilt in future fight.
periodthree The long leangle's nascent form
periodthree Forespoke the distant battle-storm;
periodthree And club and malka's embryo shape

periodthree Stood symbols there of warlike deed.
periodthree Ah! well said Uimba, sage of old,
periodthree That each tall tree its story told.
periodthree The myrtle green to wild korang 
periodthree Its bloody fate prophetic sang;
periodthree And wind-shook tchyrels, as they moaned,
periodthree The hunted emeu's end intoned.
periodthree And so the wangiem-yielding tree, 
periodthree That sighs at sunset mournfully,
periodthree Sings to the wind - whose latest breath
periodthree Stirs its lank leaves - the song of death;
periodthree And vows the vengeance man must wreak
periodthree Where sounds the wangiem's battle-shriek.

periodthree XII.
periodthree The boy delighted marked the man

periodthree Drew nearer yet, as if to ask

periodthree Became the straightest shaft that stood

periodthree And sing the wangiem-maker's song;
periodthree To mould the malka or the mace,
periodthree Arm and defence for danger's place.
periodthree In short, his brain the man imbued
periodthree Well with this maiden lesson rude.
periodthree XIII.
periodthree Mamba returned each day to view

periodthree XIV.
periodthree He came one evening from the chase
periodthree With joy upon his wearied face,
periodthree And threw in silence on the ground

periodthree Sprang to the victor-hunter's side,

periodthree And bright as sun that cleaves the cloud,

periodthree The foster-mother's duty done,
periodthree The coming day, the missing face,

periodthree Herself again without a mate,
periodthree Her bower - her bosom - desolate.
periodthree She clasped the boy until her breast,
periodthree Yielding, received the head she press'd.

periodthree XV.
periodthree Mamba! Thou learn'st these ways too fast,
periodthree The man arrives ere youth is past;
periodthree And thou - too soon - must take thy place
periodthree Among the elders of the race.
periodthree [12] I bore thee not - but oh, forgive
periodthree The heart that asks thee still to live
periodthree A while beside the little fire
periodthree That warmed 'the son without a sire'
periodthree For years, whilst thou without a peer
periodthree Hast reigned in this fond bosom here.
periodthree I bore thee not. Thy mother fled,
periodthree That thou might'st live - she sought the dead;
periodthree And I had lost (methought) my life,
periodthree When little Tono ended strife,
periodthree And turned upon his leafy bed,
periodthree Whereon I deemed my hopes lay dead.
periodthree XVI.
periodthree "No sire had I - my husband lost - 
periodthree My only bud the cruel frost
periodthree Nipp'd, ere it bloomed a beauteous flower - 
periodthree Vain was the mother's tear-drop shower.
periodthree I thought ('twas ere these lids were dry)
periodthree That life was learning but to die;
periodthree And then thy mother's hope ('twas said)
periodthree Hung by a tiny, treacherous thread.
periodthree Alas! she went - and I in grief
periodthree Sought by her corpse the strange relief
periodthree That woe to woe vouchsafes alway,
periodthree By night, and hope with dawning day:
periodthree 'Twas then I first beheld in thee
periodthree A Tono sent mysteriously.
periodthree 'Tis wrong that we aloud should name
periodthree The lost, when life's extinguished flame
periodthree No longer warms the curdled red
periodthree That chokes the pulse's silent bed.
periodthree I chose a flower - the first I found
periodthree Upon the green and blessed ground,
periodthree [13] Where new-born Mamba sighed and smiled,
periodthree And Borote gained a second child.
periodthree 'Tis thine for life; it bloomed for thee,
periodthree It smiled thy welcome pensively.
periodthree Long may it glad the much-loved plain,
periodthree And speak thy birth for years again.
periodthree And aye, where'er I build my bower,
periodthree Joy to greet the Mamba flower."
periodthree XVII.
periodthree Mamba replied with speaking eye
periodthree That beamed with love despairingly.
periodthree It told her more than tongue could tell - 
periodthree How Mamba, tho' he loved her well,
periodthree Had cast his lot among the bold
periodthree That ruled the tribe since times of old.
periodthree She sighed, and said - "My life, my joy,
periodthree My cherished, too-ambitious boy - 
periodthree The wise men soon shall call thee hence,
periodthree Despite a mother's eloquence.
periodthree But thou from her hast nought to fear - 
periodthree From her no sigh, no falling tear,
periodthree Shall come to mar the fatal plan
periodthree That makes her Mamba yet a man."
periodthree Then Mamba, softening as he spoke,
periodthree Whispered the fearful Ghimbo-boke; 
periodthree But Borote smiling shook her head,
periodthree And her voice shook as thus she said - 
periodthree "Ne'er ask of me - I know it not,
periodthree What mystery marks the manly rite;
periodthree The hour, the day, the secret spot,
periodthree The words of wisdom or of might.
periodthree But this is mine - I know it well - 
periodthree Our fathers all have passed the same;
periodthree [14] The secret, man may never tell
periodthree Till youth assumes the manly name.
periodthree And thou art brave, and bold as they
periodthree Who faced the doubtful rite before,
periodthree And rose amid the sages grey,
periodthree A man among the men of yore.
periodthree But this is why I chiefly grieve:
periodthree To think a mother's care is o'er;
periodthree A mother's words can ne'er deceive - 
periodthree Thou ne'er shalt own a mother more."
periodthree XVIII.
periodthree The tale went round, the gibe and song,
periodthree Amid the young, the tall, the strong;
periodthree And many a bright and merry eye
periodthree Flashed with a pent-up mystery.
periodthree At length young Pahmeel laughed aloud.
periodthree And Ninghim too, until he bowed
periodthree Across the broken spear he mended,
periodthree That shook until his laughter ended,
periodthree And long, deep-drawn, escaping sighs
periodthree Relieved the breast and filled the eyes.
periodthree "Ninghim!" he faltered - (and he laughed
periodthree To Pahmeel, who had only quaffed
periodthree One mouthful from his calabash, 
periodthree And set it down, lest drinking rash
periodthree Should choke him, as he rocked in glee
periodthree With hands upon his up-drawn knee) - 
periodthree "They say young Mamba's found a sire.
periodthree (Beware!) The water's in the fire!
periodthree This crystal seems bewitched, I think,
periodthree And laughs at him who fain would drink."
periodthree "A sire indeed!" quoth Burtalcaang,
periodthree Belov'd as story-tellers sang
periodthree [15] Of old, when boys forsooth had rather
periodthree Lose aught in life except a father;
periodthree "But what's a sire to him or thee
periodthree That loves to rove the forest free?
periodthree His mother - she is not his own,
periodthree His father like the summer's flown;
periodthree Say, who shall lift the Borote-yoke,
periodthree And lead him to the Ghim-boboke?
periodthree A father, and a comrade too,
periodthree A choice let's hope he'll never rue."
periodthree XIX.
periodthree To him, Pahmeel, a merry wight,
periodthree Whose large dark eyes were wild and bright - 
periodthree "Borote supplies his mother's place;
periodthree Nernepten takes him to the chase - 
periodthree Teaches him weapon-maker's art,
periodthree The warrior's and the hunter's part;
periodthree To wield the malka, stalk the game,
periodthree And burn the cover out with flame.
periodthree Methinks there's more in this than we
periodthree In all our wisdom seem to see;
periodthree Except myself and Ninghim wild,
periodthree That deem the boy Nernepten's child."
periodthree A laugh went round - "And Mamba's mother!"
periodthree Cried Bangan. "Yes! he had another;
periodthree But even Borote vows that she
periodthree Ne'er pierced that father mystery.
periodthree Borote's a foster-mother only - 
periodthree A woman by herself, and lonely,
periodthree But for the boy that shares her bower;
periodthree The name-son of a silly flower.
periodthree And brave Nernepten - for he's brave - 
periodthree Would sooner hide in mountain cave
periodthree Than where the clack of woman's tongue
periodthree Thro' all the forest mazes rung.
periodthree [16] If he did wed, we knew it not,
periodthree Nor in what wild secluded spot
periodthree He kept the wife he woo'd or stole - 
periodthree The solace of his secret soul."
periodthree XX.
periodthree "Shame on you all!" a voice exclaimed
periodthree "Shame!" flashed a pair of eyes that flamed,
periodthree And grey Terillin turned his beard
periodthree Tow'rds the wild group whose tongues were feared,
periodthree But most of all by youths and maids
periodthree That sighed o'er eyes or glossy braids;
periodthree Or chanted love-lays to the morn,
periodthree In murmurs as the day was born.
periodthree "Nernepten's brave - 'tis truly said,
periodthree And brave Nernepten wears a head
periodthree Where one, a water-drinker rash,
periodthree Wears nothing but a calabash."
periodthree With this he glanced at young Pahmeel
periodthree From heel to head, from head to heel;
periodthree And looked the cowering stripling down

periodthree "You, Ninghim, too - and Bangan bold,
periodthree Sly and deceitful yet not old;
periodthree And Burtalcaang - that wear no yoke,
periodthree Yet never knew the Ghim-boboke - 
periodthree Shame on ye all! Ye cannot see
periodthree A woman succour misery - 
periodthree A childless man take up a child,
periodthree And train its aspirations wild - 
periodthree But ye must turn and twist the tale
periodthree To laughter's ends, with words that rail.
periodthree Mark me again, ye talkers rash:
periodthree If aught can one of you abash,
periodthree It should be this - an old man's word.
periodthree That else for long had been deferred
periodthree [17] To future time and wilder scene - 
periodthree The night of Ghim-boboke Yapeen." 
periodthree XXI.
periodthree Nernepten never raised his head,
periodthree But hewed amain the wangiem red;
periodthree Nor turned with eagle eye askance
periodthree Upon the group an angry glance.
periodthree Borote heard frequent tales that flew
periodthree Around the camp: each breeze that blew
periodthree Bore in its murmur many a gibe
periodthree Against the sireless of the tribe.
periodthree But Borote, listening, only smiled,
periodthree And loved the more the changeling child
periodthree That heaven conferred, when she to earth
periodthree Consigned the infant of her birth.
periodthree XXII.
periodthree Borote, with heavy heart and sad,
periodthree Traversed the wood, where birdlings glad
periodthree Mocked with their wildest warbling song
periodthree Her thoughts of woe - her dream of wrong.
periodthree The day had come, the morn had broke,
periodthree That ushered in the "Ghim-boboke."
periodthree From woman's eye that rite is bid,
periodthree To woman is the thought forbid
periodthree To pierce the cloud that veils the light
periodthree Of manhood merging into might.
periodthree Alas! 'Tis sad to grieve alone - 
periodthree To know one's chiefest joy is flown;
periodthree But doubly sad to see the sun
periodthree Of woe's first day, but just begun,
periodthree Smile on the face bedewed with tears,
periodthree And laughing, dart a ray that sears
periodthree [18] The heart that aches in deep'ning sorrow,
periodthree Expectant of a dark to-morrow.
periodthree XXIII.
periodthree Mamba remote and silent sate
periodthree Secluded, like the youths who wait
periodthree The bidding of the tribal sires
periodthree To join them by the myst'ry fires,
periodthree Not ours the wisdom nor the light
periodthree To shadow forth that solemn rite;
periodthree Nor what the word, nor what the way,
periodthree That moulds a man from boyish clay.
periodthree *  *  * * *
periodthree XXIV.
periodthree Let it suffice - the rite was o'er;
periodthree They led him to the river shore,
periodthree Whose grassy curves wound in and out
periodthree Between the tree-trunks tall and stout.
periodthree Headlong he plunged, came out again,
periodthree Shook from his locks the river rain,
periodthree And stood between his guard and guide
periodthree A new-made man, in all his pride,
periodthree Flowers on his brow, a golden wreath,
periodthree They placed: his bright eyes beamed beneath;
periodthree And thus, with nodding blossoms crowned,
periodthree They homewards led the "newly-found."
periodthree XXV.
periodthree Terillin rose - the grave, the grey - 
periodthree And met the comers on their way;
periodthree Advancing, took the crown'd one's hand,
periodthree And led him tow'rds the snow-capped band,
periodthree "Fathers!" he cried, "I bring with me
periodthree One pass'd the ancient mystery,
periodthree That ye and I, and all the old
periodthree Have known, but ne'er to stranger told.
periodthree [19] He comes, a man amongst our men - 
periodthree Heaven send us such a one again!
periodthree What, though no father's name he bears,
periodthree Nor badge of father's bravery wears,
periodthree Shall he be less among his peers
periodthree Because as yet unfleshed his spears?
periodthree Did Burtalcaang, who bears no yoke,
periodthree E'er face the dreaded Ghim-boboke?
periodthree Or Pahmeel, whose wild laughter rings

periodthree Ninghim, or Bangan, can they say
periodthree Mamba's without a sire to-day?
periodthree His sire behold! Am I not he - 
periodthree His father in the mystery?
periodthree XXVI.
periodthree Nameless should be the silent dead 
periodthree (And here Terillin bowed his head);
periodthree But, though all nameless in the dust,
periodthree To nameless memory be just.
periodthree His father was the gallant son
periodthree Whom glory from affection won.
periodthree When, waking once from dreams of joy,
periodthree They told me I had lost my boy,
periodthree Red was my spear and red my hand - 
periodthree I raised the camp with fiery brand;

periodthree I could not bring him back again.
periodthree Childless for long, I see my son,
periodthree His life as 'twere again begun.
periodthree But I am old, unnerved, and grey,
periodthree And half my strength is snatched away.
periodthree [20] Thus to Nernepten I bequeath
periodthree The boy who wears the golden wreath.
periodthree Behold in me thy sires proud sire;
periodthree Embrace me, boy! join fire to fire."
periodthree This to young Mamba, as he flew
periodthree Into the arms of grandsire true.
periodthree Pahmeel and Ninghim hung the head;
periodthree The history round the camp-fire spread
periodthree And Bangan bold and Burtalcaang
periodthree Each felt of burning shame the pang.
periodthree XXVII.
periodthree "'Twas glorious - yes! but was it well
periodthree (Cried Taalar) of the dead to tell?
periodthree To raise again from where it rests
periodthree The secret buried in our breasts - 
periodthree The woe felt when our hero slain
periodthree Victorious fell on Ryndia's plain?
periodthree Oh! Death may chance to be forespoke,
periodthree E'en at our solemn Ghim-boboke.
periodthree And though, methink, a brave grandsire
periodthree Sits next him by the mystery fire;
periodthree And though his sire at last is known - 
periodthree Albeit his burning soul is flown - 
periodthree Mamba may never live to mourn
periodthree Terillin from his children torn."
periodthree This, hoarsely whispered by Taalar,
periodthree All silent else both near and far;
periodthree And Mamba, 'mid the elders placed,
periodthree Sate while his face with lines they traced.
periodthree XXVIII.
periodthree The day had fled, the moon arose,
periodthree Night straight began with evening's close - 
periodthree A night whose calm and silvery sheen
periodthree Befitted well the wild yapeen.
periodthree [21] Within the circle of the camp
periodthree Blazed the clear fire, while measured tramp
periodthree Of dancing warriors shook the ground,
periodthree To song and time-sticks' throbbing sound.
periodthree There twice two hundred feet advanced,
periodthree There twice a hundred malkas glanced
periodthree Bright in the moon, that silvered o'er
periodthree The arms that all those malkas bore.
periodthree Wild the device, and strange the sign
periodthree That stared in many a snowy line
periodthree From beaming face and heaving breast,
periodthree And limbs that seldom paused to rest;
periodthree Whilst all the rib-like lines laid on,
periodthree Made each man seem a skeleton.
periodthree Nodded the feathers from the red
periodthree And netted band that bound each head,

periodthree The cadence of the song they sang;
periodthree And every face and limb below,
periodthree And tree above them, caught the glow
periodthree That spread from camp-fire's rising blaze,
periodthree Lighting the yapeen's wond'rous maze
periodthree Of feet and ankles in the dance
periodthree With fitful gleam or twinkling glance.
periodthree XXIX.
periodthree Conspicuous 'mid the dancing crowd,
periodthree Whose ranks alternate swayed and bowed,
periodthree Shone Mamba, tricked with wild design,
periodthree And symbol traced in waving line.
periodthree No limbs more active wore the green
periodthree At yon great Ghim-boboke yapeen;
periodthree And no two arms more graceful there

periodthree Drank in the sight, the joy, the sound;
periodthree And Mamba's form throughout the dance
periodthree Attracted every wondering glance.
periodthree Borote! She viewed him and she wept - 
periodthree Proud of her son; and then she crept
periodthree Alone into the darkness wild,
periodthree And there bewailed her sundered child.
periodthree Out far beyond the camp leant she
periodthree Her aching head against a tree;
periodthree The fires behind her brightly burned,
periodthree The turf the dancers lightly spurned;
periodthree And thro' the forest, laughter rang,
periodthree As all the sitting matrons sang,
periodthree To "time-stick" cadence by the fire,
periodthree The joy of him "that lacked a sire."
periodthree "Ah me!" groaned Borote, "is it well
periodthree That I should live the tale to tell
periodthree Of love bestowed and love returned,
periodthree Love lost again, or all unlearned?
periodthree That I - the only joy he knew - 
periodthree False to myself, to him still true,
periodthree Should here alone with salt tears flow,
periodthree Weep o'er his joy and call it woe?"
periodthree She sobbed; the tears ran down apace - 
periodthree Blent in each other on her face,
periodthree Like sorrows such as seldom come
periodthree Alone - but join and make the sum
periodthree Of one vast melting, burning grief,
periodthree That ever brings its own relief,
periodthree She wept, and found her heart's distress
periodthree Worthless and worse than nothingness;
periodthree Reproached herself, and yet she sighed,
periodthree As her sweet streaming face she dried;
periodthree [23] And passing to her bower alone,
periodthree With dragging foot and fitful moan,
periodthree Paused sadly by the ashes there,
periodthree For the dark hearth was cold and bare;
periodthree Then laid her down, all lost in woe.
periodthree Her lullaby the river's flow.
periodthree Grief brought it's balm - now past the worst,
periodthree And all the river-murmurs nurst
periodthree Her soul to sleep, nor sent a dream,
periodthree Nor yet of joy nor hope a gleam.
periodthree *  *  * * *
periodthree Suns set, and many a changing moon
periodthree Shone on the sad one all too soon;
periodthree Tho' Mamba still increased in grace,
periodthree Whilst the bright radiance of his face,
periodthree Was foremost theme with young and old - 
periodthree His port the envy of the bold;
periodthree A mighty, stalwart hunter he
periodthree Fit hero for camp minstrelsy.
periodthree XXX.
periodthree The bright-eyed Mamba on the trail
periodthree Followed his quarry 'gainst the gale;
periodthree Outstripped in flight the swift korang
periodthree His dogs, with late ensanguined fang;
periodthree And every breeze that eastward blew
periodthree Bore on its wings the boy's halloo,
periodthree As crying eager to his hounds
periodthree The hills sent back the cheery sounds;
periodthree The shout, the barking chorus rang
periodthree Till all the grim, grey forest sang,
periodthree And rustling leaves, and boughs that bent
periodthree Joined in the airy merriment.
periodthree The youth was not unseen. His track
periodthree For miles, for leagues, behind his back,
periodthree [24] Hard followed by an anxious few,
periodthree Gave hopes of victim soon in view.
periodthree Mamba, with hunter's practised ear,
periodthree Caught the first sounds as man drew near
periodthree And standing motionless and still,
periodthree He silent scanned the glade and hill,
periodthree Revolving in his mind what chance
periodthree Might next require his spear or lance.
periodthree XXXI.
periodthree Scarce out of sight, with heads to wind,
periodthree With listening ears to turf inclined,
periodthree There crouched a mute and murderous band
periodthree That Mamba's swift destruction plann'd.
periodthree They rose, by turns, on hands and knees,
periodthree Peered through the brushwood and the trees,
periodthree Saw the tall plume on Mamba's head,
periodthree But heard no more his springy tread;
periodthree For Mamba, warned by air-borne sound,
periodthree And pointed ear of whining hound,
periodthree Stood like a statue, black as night,
periodthree Relieved against a flood of light.
periodthree The broad sun smiled on bad and good,
periodthree On swift pursuer and pursued;
periodthree One golden gleam the follower caught,
periodthree The followed seeker and the sought.
periodthree *  *  * * *
periodthree XXXII.
periodthree Sudden before young Mamba stood,
periodthree With green branch riven from the wood,
periodthree A figure tall, athletic, dark,
periodthree All knotted, sinewy, stout and stark -

periodthree That emblem'd friendship might be seen
periodthree But Mamba still uncertain gazed
periodthree Upon the flutt'ring symbol raised,
periodthree [25] Yet dropped his stout death-dealing spear,
periodthree As scorning to acknowledge fear.
periodthree The foe (for foe it was) drew nigh

periodthree Neuarpur - Apsley
periodthree Victoria
periodthree 19th February 1867 
periodthree My dear Miss Lewin, 
periodthree On arriving at Melbourne I sent you an Argus containing an account of the voyage made by the Swiftside which was a very pleasant & favourable one though a little longer than was expected being exactly 12 weeks. I hope you received the Argus else you will think it very strange never having heard anything of me. We only remained in Melbourne from Friday to Tuesday. My brother was there waiting for me. On Christmas Day we began our journey up the Country - went by rail to Ballarat. There Mr Hines' brother-in-law met us, we made all one party & were 12 in number. We drove up about 260 miles - used to start very early in the morning, rest in the heat of the day & make another start in the evening - the weather was very hot, more so than has been felt for the last 4 years. We had all kinds of adventures in the shape of kicking horses & broken poles but we reached Benyeo (the residence of Mr McLeod - brother-in-law to Mr Hines) on the following Sunday. [191] [192]
periodthree It is 14 miles distant from this place - Mrs Hines & I were over here for a day or two - made all right for the children to come - but when we returned to Benyeo for them, Mrs Hines took measles & from that day which was not a week after we reached Benyeo up to the present there has been nothing but sickness. Just as Mrs H. was over the worst of measles the eldest girl was taken ill the day after her 12th birthday. She was affected very strangely & tho' a Doctor was sent for at once it was 48 hours before one arrived. Then Bessie was dangerously ill with inflammation of the lungs - about 10 days after she was first attacked measles came out on her slightly - the Doctors (for now there were two) thought she might now get better but her strength was all gone & she gradually sank & died at Benyeo last Saturday, exactly the day month of her birthday when she appeared in her usual health.
periodthree Her death has cast a great gloom on everything. She was a gentle companionable intellectual child liked by everyone who knew her - the second girl misses her sadly - Bessie was laid beside a brother in a small burying place adjoining the garden on Sunday & on Monday we all came over here for good - Every one at Benyeo who had not had measles before had them during the six weeks we were there - 15 cases in all. Fortunately I had had them & was able to look after some of the invalids.
periodthree I like the people I have met in Australia much better than I like what I have yet seen of the country but it is too soon to judge - I have experienced nothing but kindness from Mr & Mrs H. all through but particularly lately. We have done nothing yet with lessons - they brought out a beautiful piano, the only thing poor Mrs Hines now cares about - she idolized her eldest child. As soon as I receive any money I will remit it to you. Please give my kind compliments to Miss Rye,
periodthree hoping she & you are well I remain dear Miss Lewin Very truly yours,
periodthree L. Geoghegan

periodthree Neuarpur - Apsley
periodthree Victoria
periodthree 18th October 1867
periodthree My dear Miss Lewin,
periodthree I am very glad I came to Australia, but I cannot say I like it very much. It is such an out of the world place and so monotonous, but as far as kind treatment goes I could not meet with nor desire kinder - with no one in this neighbourhood have I seen the social distinctions made with Governesses that there is at home - I have very little work here in comparison with London - I do not think £80 per annum here as much as £60 at home, dress is very expensive and the people are dressy - You will be glad to hear that my pupil has made great progress in all her studies but particularly in music, which pleases Mrs Hines very much. They brought out a very nice piano. [193]
periodthree In fact 'Bush life' is a strange mixture of roughing and refinement. In this district are two distinct sets, one gentry, and one would-be gentry - there are more of the latter. In the former I think an unfinished unladylike Governess would be unwelcome. Literature is much more brought forward here, in the general way, than at home because there are no new daily topics - the standing one is sheep - in which ladies take no part - of course.
periodthree Accept my kind regards
periodthree and believe me truly yours
periodthree Louisa Agnes Geoghegan

periodthree March 18 / 67 
periodthree Dear Father 
periodthree I received your letter dated December 11th and was delighted to hear you Mother and all my Brothers and Sisters are well and all old frends as this leaves me at presant and all the Children thanks be to God for his Kind mercy to us. [317] I was sorry to hear of the trouble my Uncle has met with by the death of his Son and also Mr Kernans Children hopeing the are now better. 
periodthree Dear Father I thought by this time I would be Sending you a better account of Brisbane but I am Sorry to Say that it has not improved Since I wrote to you last. If any it is worse; there are a grate many leaving hear for America. I Could not Complain So much of this place untill up to the presant for the buisnes I was at I had to leave on the 8th of January. I happened with an accident. I was loadeing on top of the van. The Horse Started off and I was upset & was very Severly hurt and my Colar bone was broken. I must give thanks to God I am now better. I was under a good dale of expences togeather with the loss of time it has Came very heavy on me. I am not in any employment at presant. I now want a frend to assist m[e] to get over the presant difaculty untill Such time as I would be able to make Some recompence. I was getting on to my wishes untill I happened with the accident but when I was not Killed on the Spot I have not much Cause to Complain when God was pleased to leave me over my Children. I was for two hours after that fall that I did not make a motion but lay quite Sinceless. I was takeing to my home where I had to remain for Seven weeks without leaveing my bead and the grater part of that time in Sever agony. 
periodthree Michael mentioned he would Send me a paper but I did not receive it. I would have Sent you one this time but ther is nothing in them worth reeding. As to Thos. Brady he has left Brisbane and went to Melborn about four months past. I have herd from him once Since. He was then in good health. I have had the pleasure of seeing James Murtagh at Christmas and he Came to See me when I was hurt. He wishes to be Kindly remembered to you all. He told me to mention he was to send Something to his Father and in Concequence of the dullness of the times he will not be able to Send him anything Sooner than July and that he would Send him what he Could. He is married and has three Children and the enjoy good health. He also told me that if his Brother and Sister wished to Come to this Colony he would pay there passage on Conditions that the would pay him back and if his Father wished to Come he would also pay his. 
periodthree I send m[y] love to you and Mother and all my Brothers and Sisters also to Mr McDonnell and Mr Kernan hopeing the and there family are well. Wishing to be Kindly remembered to W. S. Garnett Esqr. Mrs Garnett and family also Mrs Ryan and family Patrick Christy a[n]d Anne Gibney hopeing the all enjoy good health. I now Conclude Sending my love and blessing to you all. 
periodthree I remain Dear Father and Mother Your affectionate Son 
periodthree Christopher Dunne [318]

periodthree MR PARKES said: I am sure I express the feelings of my colleague as well as of myself, when I say that we are deeply gratified by the kind and cordial manner in which you have drunk this toast. We were told when we were invited to this entertainment that the gentlemen inviting us were colonists of New South Wales - gentlemen having a deep interest in the prosperity of that colony. This circumstance invests the present gathering with peculiar interest, because we ought not to forget - and I admit it freely and generously - that we are assembled in the capital of another colony, which is at the same time the greatest city in Australasia. The circumstance that we, the members of the Government of New South Wales - the parent of all the colonies - are met in this room in so cordial a manner by our fellow colonists, is one that I regard with special interest. In returning thanks for the compliment you have paid us, I set a special value Upon this circumstance. Our worthy friend the chairman - and I am sure you must be wise men to place this gentleman in the chair - has told us pretty distinctly the occupation in which you are all engaged. [438] I give our worthy friend the utmost credit for ingenuity and good nature; but if he expects me to make any serious revelations regarding the land policy of the Government, I fear he will be disappointed. If in the exercise of his bounteous good nature he has any design of tying me to a buggy and carrying me on to Fort Bourke, in order that I may acquire a knowledge of Riverine interests, all I can say is, he will not catch me on the other side of the Murray. I appreciate his kindness but would rather be excused from his services. Gentlemen, considering the few opportunities that I have had of understanding the country with which you are more particularly identified, considering that I have no personal interest in common with yours, I think there are few persons who have shown more consideration for the exceptional circumstances of the Border districts, or more sincere anxiety to do all that can be fairly done to place you on a level with the people of the other portions of New South Wales. On the question of the Border duties I have always felt very strongly the impolicy of collecting those duties along the River Murray. Years ago, before they were collected in accordance with law - for nothing could be more irregular than their collection at that time - I felt that if continued for any length of time they would be fraught with such serious evils that it would be better to lose the revenue than risk the danger of their collection. I have always regarded the establishment of inland Custom-houses as a positive evil which no circumstances could to any great extent modify or decrease, and I would rather have assented to any imaginable arrangements than see a whole body of custom-house officers stationed along the narrow river dividing the territory of Victoria from New South Wales. We know that the duties entrusted to officers at a remote distance from the central authority are seldom well performed; but however well they may be carried out, they must necessarily and inevitably lead to bickerings, to bad feeling, to much of that kind of evasion of the law which, if it goes on for any length of time, settles down into the inveterate vice of smuggling; and rather than see a numerous class of petty smugglers disseminating the virus of their bad habits and disaffected feeling throughout society along the banks of a river like the Murray I would submit to almost any conceivable law. This is and always has been and always will be my view of the question. I expressed this view to the colonists on both sides of the Murray when I had the honour of visiting those districts during last year; and I am sure my honourable colleague will say that I did not lose any opportunity of enforcing those views upon the Government on my return to Sydney With regard to distant portions of these Australian colonies, I am one of those who believe that where self-government can be carried out it is better that it should be carried out. [439] I am a colonist sufficiently old to remember the time when the country which is now the colony of Victoria was part of the colony of New South Wales. I took some interest in public life when the agitation was going on for the separation of this portion of the territory. I was in this city of Melbourne on the very day when the separation from New South Wales was celebrated, and all my sympathies were with my fellow-colonists in this part of the territory. I thought it was only just to them, and must necessarily be beneficial to the whole of the population, that they should be separated from the old colony and erected into a separate community. Later still I was in the Legislature of the colony when the separation of Queensland took place, and if anyone chooses to search the records of Parliament he will find that my vote was recorded for motions previously made in favour of the separation of that colony. I believe that persons considerable in numbers, considerable in property, and considerable in their industrial enterprises, who are carrying on the work of colonisation at a remote distance of 600 or 700 miles from the seat of Government, should be allowed as they attain to numerical strength sufficient for the purpose - and if other circumstances conform to such a condition of things - to form a colony of themselves. I have great sympathy for any class of my fellow-colonists who are placed under the disadvantages and difficulties which remoteness from the seat of Government will at all times carry with it. I should not like to be misunderstood or to be supposed, even by implication, to be the advocate for the creation of a new colony to be called Riverina. However earnest some gentlemen may be as Riverine patriots, I am sure they will not be displeased with me for candidly declaring my own sentiments; and I do think that the colony of New South Wales, within the boundaries fixed by the Constitution Act under which we now live, has not yet been proved to be too large. I think, before we split up any portion of this territory, we should try better than we hitherto have done - and this I confess candidly - to govern these outlying districts satisfactorily and beneficially for the whole community. I think the Government in Sydney ought to devote all its energies, without the loss of a single year to connecting the metropolis of the colony with those districts by railway. I am bound to acknowledge that one of the finest and 'noblest examples of statesmanship that I know of in the Australian colonies is the conception of the Victorian railway from Melbourne to Echuca, and the vigorous action of the Government in carrying it out to completion. I don't know who were the authors of that scheme; but I think it was sagacious in conception, and that it has been carried out with true patriotism; and I give the colony of Victoria every credit for its far-sightedness in this great work. But I should like to see the Government of New South Wales do something more than copy that example. [440] I should like to see the parent colony putting forth all her spirit of enterprise, and constructing a railway to the Murrumbidgee with even double the energy of her ardent offspring. I should go further even than this. I should be disposed to devote all the revenue derived from those outlying districts in the interior to their improvement. I believe it is a sound principle to dedicate the revenue derived from the public lands of a new country to the improvement of that country, and that the mere expenditure incurred in carrying on the civil government should be met by the ordinary means of taxation. The land once alienated can never be alienated again, and the revenue derived from that source is collected once and for all. I think, therefore, it is a correct principle that the Governments of these new countries should devote the whole of this revenue to making the land more accessible for the purposes of settlement and civilisation. I held this doctrine years ago, and I hold it still. At all times I shall be prepared to support the doctrine with reference to the outlying districts of the country. Our worthy chairman has alluded to the occasion which has brought my honourable colleague and myself to the city of Melbourne; and I am sure you possess that interest which intelligent men must feel in anything which draws the colonies into closer intercourse and into a better understanding. For my own part, I do not hesitate to say that I regard this occasion - though I am in no sense the author of it - as one full of interest, as one from which much may be expected, and from which I believe many good results will undoubtedly flow. For the first time in the history of these Australian colonies they have all assembled, including New Zealand - I may say all of them, because they are all represented, with the exception of Western Australia - with no feeling of emulation less worthy than the desire to have the largest share in effecting a common end to promote their common interests. It appears to me a very important occasion; and from my intercourse with the gentlemen who have been entrusted with this important mission I have formed so good an opinion of their judgment, of their sound understanding, and of their disinterested desire to promote the good of the entire group of colonies, to lose sight of individual interests as far as they can be lost sight of consistently with a proper feeling of patriotism; that, although I am restricted from saying anything about our proceedings, I think I may venture to say that the results will not fail to be satisfactory to the Australian people, and productive of great good to the Australian family. periodthree My dear Miss Lewin, I am now so reconciled to Australia that I was surprised to see by your letter I had apparently been disappointed at first. At times I feel it is rather dull work never to go beyond the garden or Croquet ground but then I remember I can rake or hoe in the garden as I please & freedom to please oneself more than compensates for monotony. Occasionally we have a good deal of riding, & I have a nice horse for my own use - then if Mr Hines is busy we are sometimes weeks without going outside the gates.
periodthree Latterly there has been a great deal of gaiety for this place - one public Ball & two private ones - one of the private ones here. The style is to dance till daylight, because it is impossible to ride or drive in the dark, so those who must go, dance until it is light enough to start & the rest take thankfully anything they can get in the shape of a bed - when it comes to provide for thirty you cannot be very particular. [194]
periodthree I felt the heat much more this summer than last - but then it was more continued. & unusually severe - this part is nearly as hot as Adelaide - I hope this Xmas to be able to take a trip to my brother & sister. Travelling there is very very expensive & last year I felt economical - I remain dear Miss Lewin
periodthree Very truly yours

periodthree Dear Miss Lewin, I am so glad that my gratitude has caused you pleasure - but it did not half acknowledge what I feel or the benefit you have done me - I cannot tell you anything about the wants of Melbourne - except that I see in the Melbourne Newspapers accounts of a Society for 'Educated people in Indigent Circumstances', their applications to the Society published etc, & teachers of both sexes figure largely in the list.
periodthree In this district (colonial term) for three gentlemen there are six mushrooms, I suppose you would call them. The former I have heard say would like thoroughly good lady Governess from Home if they had any one there conscientiously to select them - the mushroom class pay largely but expect rather queer things - viz that the Governess should light the Schoolroom fire & similar things. They have been accustomed themselves to manual exertions & dont understand not keeping it up. In my short experience, I have known of two cases where ladies got with these people & very soon had to separate.
periodthree It is a totally different life from what it is at home. In nearly every instance you are looked on as the Intellectual Member of the Establishment. You are the constant companion & associate of the Lady - considered, I might say indulged, in every way - & your only difficulty is to civilize the children, which you are supposed to do through example as they are uncontrolled to a degree, & the parents object to anything else. I believe in Adelaide salaries are much lower than in Victoria.
periodthree I think with you that capable women have a better chance here than at home [196] - but I think a few of a good class not long accustomed to home scrubbing & drudgery would be a better importation than a larger number of the common run of Governesses - I think it a mistake unless very strong minded to come out here without having some relatives in the Colony - no out-door variety - no change of face or scene - so that the feeling of monotony & exile is apt to take forcible possession of you, unless you know you have a resource to shake it off. My thoughts on the subject may be very imperfect ones for I have never given it deliberate consideration. [195]
periodthree I remain dear Miss Lewin

periodthree We are here in a country endowed with enormous wealth, with a large surface of rich territory, which it is now our object, and has been for years, to distribute, as justly as we can, among the great bulk of the people who desire to settle upon that land, at a price lower than its market value. [116] That is our desire. Now what is the difficulty with which any people or any Government having this object in view is immediately met? The difficulty is the competition of capital. In that struggle of capital against those who have no capital, whom it is desired to endow with a portion of the advantages resulting from the public possession of the lands, capital is always sure to gain the victory. If you enact legal provisions by which you direct every person who wants a piece of land worth £100 to get it, by means of legal machinery, for £50, and if the poor man, in availing himself of this legal means of obtaining the land, is exposed to the competition of the rich man, who can doubt who will be successful? In such a competition the few will always overcome the many. Wealth will always outstrip poverty; and fraud will always outweigh simplicity. Surely experience has confirmed these observations, which would arise a priori if we had no experience to guide us. Has not all our experience in land legislation in this country shown that, unless there be an arbitrary power outside the courts of law - not dependent upon any legal machinery either for its existence, or for the means of carrying out its decrees - those who are eager to obtain land, and are willing to obtain it by unjust and fraudulent means, if assisted and backed by capital, will always succeed in getting it, to the prevention of the poorer man, who, without capital, seeks to obtain a share of this advantage? All our land legislation has failed, so far as it has failed, simply from this cause.
periodthree It is idle to say that land legislation can meet and defeat the various contrivances of fraud. Those contrivances are so numerous, and the means of resisting them, if absolute power be not given, so weak, that - I care not how carefully your Acts are framed - if men are tempted by strong inducements of avarice, and are provided with legal means to effect their object, the State will be defrauded, and the poor man for whom you wish to legislate will be utterly defeated. Therefore, I avow that while I regard these large powers i.e. for the Minister as an essential part of this Bill, I am prepared to support the Bill because it contains these powers, and I should not be prepared to support any Land Bill which did not contain them.

periodthree I believe that there are now close upon 20,000 persons holding licences under the 42nd section, the area of their land being about 486,000 acres; and under the 12th section there' are 10,000 or 12,000 persons holding licences for 1,425,000 acres. All this settlement has taken place since the Land Act of 1865 came into operation. The value of the improvements made on the land taken up under the 12th section amounts to £1,500,000. I may also mention, as showing the bona fides of the selectors, that the revenue to be received from rentals (leases and licences) under the sections to which I have referred, for the year 1868, was estimated by the present Government at £220,000, and by the Sladen Government at £205,000; but up to the present time the amount received is £227,000, or £5,000 in excess of our estimate [...]. [136]
periodthree We no longer hear of swagmen tramping from one end of the territory to the other - going from station to station, and from place to place, as mere idlers and loafers. They have now settled down, having got little plots of ground from the Government. We do not now hear of so many wandering miners, many of the mining population having settled down on the land. The settlement which has taken place on the gold-fields is something surprising. By the facilities which have been afforded for settlement of that character some of the best classes of colonists have been attached to our soil, who would otherwise have been wanderers up and down upon the face of the earth. There are also many men - hundreds of them, to my certain knowledge - who, having made money in the colony in business, and in various walks of life, have invested their savings in these holdings, who would otherwise, most probably, have taken themselves and their money out of the colony. These, sir, are the fruits of the legislation which we were enabled to effect by the assistance of the great Liberal party who now sit in this House, who have supported us most disinterestedly, most patriotically, and with great sacrifice to themselves during the last three years. They have not only supported us in our various struggles to accomplish the settlement of the people on the land, but they have supported us in the great constitutional struggles in which this House has been engaged. To them it must be a very pleasant reflection that by their assistance we have at all events been able to accomplish some good. We have not left this colony the worse for being intrusted with the administration of the land law and the general government of the country during the last six years. Our administration is not only bearing fruit now, but I believe it will bear fruit when we are sleeping in the dust.

periodthree Will you shortly state what you consider the obstacles in the way of still further supplementing the resources of this district through selection? - It may be my own opinion only - it is that the selections are too small. It is a mistake to keep married women from being allowed to select; 320 acres is not enough for a married man - I think a man and his wife ought to be able to select. In the first place, by encouraging single people to select and keeping those who get married from selecting, it discourages marriage in the colony and keeps down the population, and may cause the Government to say some day we want immigrants, when here you have the bone and muscle of the colony.
periodthree Can you say that there is any decided increase in the production of grain in this district? - Yes; every year.
periodthree Do you remember the number of bushels of wheat raised here in the first year that you took the statistics? - I could not remember what it was.
periodthree Is there any record? - No; we are not allowed to keep a record, and there is a penalty of £10 for making an extract.
periodthree Do you keep no records in the department? - No; I collect them and forward them to the Government, and I am liable to a fine if I make any extracts.
periodthree I presume we can get the whole of the returns by applying to the Government for them? - Yes.
periodthree You remember, at any rate, that a great increase has taken place in wheat? - Yes.
periodthree Has the increase of production kept pace with the increase of selection? [147] - More so. Those who had 30 or 40 acres under crop the first year had 100 and 150 the second and third years.
periodthree Is the farming class prosperous and successful, would you say? - I should say not - they have not had time.
periodthree And yet the production has enormously increased? - Yes,
periodthree Can you explain that? - There have been several dry seasons and the number of bushels per acre has not been fairly remunerative - only 8 or 10 bushels to the acre this last season.
periodthree What was the average three years ago? - I cannot remember, but it was better than that. I have cut 35 bushels of wheat to the acre here myself.
periodthree What is the wheat sold at here? - I cannot tell you.
periodthree What were the circumstances under which you obtained so good a return? - It was not exceptionally rich land, it was a sand-hill.
periodthree It was a good wheat year, I suppose? - Not extraordinarily.
periodthree I suppose you had enough rain - more than last year or the year before? - Yes.
periodthree You value the various holdings? - Yes.
periodthree You mentioned that you would like to see the holdings increased from 320 acres to 640 acres; in this district, on the ordinary land, can a man make a good living out of 320 acres? - A single man may, starting with fair means, but a married man, with a family of small children, it is a misery to him.
periodthree Are there many farms occupied by single men in this district? - A good few.
periodthree Can you give an idea of how many? - No.
periodthree Are they numerous? - I cannot say that. They are principally steady young men; but there are cases of men with a wife and small family who are deeply in debt.
periodthree Will it improve the position of the man in difficulty to have a larger farm to improve - would not that increase his difficulty? - Not supposing he had 640 acres to start off with. It does not take double the number of rods of fencing for 640 acres that it does to fence 320, and he can keep sheep enough to support him while he is making-improvements, grubbing and so forth.
periodthree But there is the objection, that if he takes 640 acres there will be less for others? - I cannot mention a case where a man who has a family of young children is doing well.
periodthree What do you mean by well? - Paying his way; keeping out of debt.
periodthree After so short a time with his improvements to make, house and so on, and commencing without capital, it is unreasonable to expect him to be in good circumstances? - Yes, quite so; but if he gets into debt he cannot get out again with 320 acres. He is deeper in debt every day. [148]
periodthree Have you had experience in any other district? - No. I have been here twenty-eight years.
periodthree Then you look forward not hopefully to the present settlement in this district, owing to the small areas? - In the case of families of small children.
periodthree If they work themselves and all put their shoulder to the wheel, 320 acres seems to be a sufficient holding? - With only one shoulder to the wheel it is hard work, with so many mouths to feed.
periodthree If they are the right stamp they will get on. The idea of the State is not to make a wealthy man, but a comfortable man? - Well, I wish you were round with me sometimes.
periodthree You cannot do it all at once? - After three or four years, and the man in debt to the full value of his selection, he will never be comfortable. I know cases where with 640 acres they would have been able to pay their way.
periodthree Do they give that as the reason? - Yes, some do.
periodthree Then, suppose you make it 1,280 acres, would not that be better?
periodthree Yes; double it again, that would be better still.
periodthree Has the increased production arisen from increased settlement, or how? - In this way. In every selection taken up there is some wheat put down, if not the first year the second year, and then more the next year, from 40 acres up to 100 and 150.
periodthree As a rule the selectors are cultivating more yearly? - Yes.
periodthree From your conversations with the selectors, are you of opinion that there is a tendency to sell out after they secure their lease? - No, generally not; they are as a rule anxious to make a home for themselves. There are a few exceptions.
periodthree You have said that the selectors are as a rule in difficulties, that it is almost impossible for a man with a young family to succeed, and that those who have fallen into financial difficulties cannot get out - how are they then to be retained on the land? - I think there is very little hope for a great many of them.
periodthree Have any of these people you spoke to told you they will have to sell out because they cannot pay their liabilities incurred in past years? - Yes.
periodthree Have they told you that they have been threatened that they will be sold out unless they pay their debts? - Yes.
periodthree If they had got money on better terms, would that have been sufficient to keep them out of difficulty? - I think it would.
periodthree If, instead of borrowing at 22 per cent. on their licences, they were able to borrow from the State at something like 8 per cent. the difficulty would be easily overcome? - I believe so. There are many now who are deeply in debt, who, if they could get the money at 8 per cent., would still struggle through.
periodthree Have you heard many complaints made as to the high charges for money? - They say they have to pay pretty stiff for money, and also for rations and food, from the storekeepers. [149]
periodthree Is it a cash trade or a credit trade here? - It is all credit trade here.
periodthree Have you heard that because of the excessive charges- they will be ultimately driven from the land? - Yes.
periodthree I suppose the whole trade here is so entirely credit that any one coming here to open a cash business would not make it pay? - I think he might succeed in time.
periodthree Are not the customers secured by having them on the books?? - Yes; but there are some others.
periodthree Are not the prices, owing to the credit system, higher here than the working classes elsewhere have to pay? - Yes. I know for a fact that the storekeepers give a very long time, and charge high in consequence.
periodthree And make a good profit? - Yes.
periodthree What is the difference between the charges here and in Geelong or Melbourne? - Fifty per cent, higher here. Take a pair of moleskin trousers. In Stawell you can buy them for 5s. or 5s. 6d. a pair; here, in Horsham, they are 10s. and 11s.
periodthree You attribute that difference exclusively to the fact of the credit trade here? - Yes, I must say in Stawell you have to pay cash.
periodthree Did you ever buy a pair of moleskin trousers yourself? - No; I speak only from hearsay.
periodthree I think you make a mistake about that - moleskin trousers could not be bought for that price anywhere? - It is only what I heard.
periodthree You think that the Government, having provided the selectors with cheap land, should also provide them with cheap money to keep them on the land? - The great majority start with nothing, and go there as a last resource.
periodthree Would a reduction of the yearly rent to half the present amount - 1s. an acre instead of 2s. - be a substantial relief? - Not for those who are deeply in debt - £16 a year would do no good.
periodthree In fact, these people you speak of are not redeemable? - Some of them are. 
periodthree Are there many in that state? - Not a great many.
periodthree Fifty per cent, to the storekeeper, and 22.5 per cent. To the money lender - that would explain everything without the smallness of the holding? - Yes; but if the holding had been larger to start with they would not have required the accommodation.
periodthree I suppose the storekeepers are very rich men up here? - I do not think so; bad debts do not make rich men.

periodthree 26. Will you explain how the sittings and business of the Supreme Court are regulated? They are regulated in reference to the state of the business of the court, the terms, the insolvency days, the equity days, and the circuits. [206]
periodthree 27. Have the judges the sole power of regulating that business? Yes; that is inherent in every court. 1 may add, though, that, by statute, the Governor in Council has power to appoint the places where the assizes shall he held leaving the judges the power to name the times when they shall he held.
periodthree 28. In reference to the appointing of times, is the Bar, or the legal profession generally, consulted - is their convenience consulted? Their convenience is certainly consulted by the action of the judges; but they are not personally consulted. On one or two occasions, when the arrangement was found to be inconvenient, a representation was made to the judges, and the following year the arrangement was altered. For instance, we used to go up to Maryborough before we went to Rockhampton; and that was found to be rather inconvenient. There was a good deal of time to spare at Maryborough, and very little at Rockhampton; and it was thought that the holiday would come best at the close of the circuit.
periodthree 29. Are you aware, Judge Lutwyche, that complaints are made by the Bar, and the other branch of the legal profession, that their convenience is not sufficiently consulted? I am not aware of it.
periodthree 30. What are the usual hours of sitting in your court or courts? In term time, ten o'clock till four, with an interval of adjournment - generally half-an-hour. At the sittings in assize, from ten o'clock till any hour the presiding judge thinks proper to sit, with the usual interval of adjournment of an hour for lunch. In insolvency, from eleven o'clock to four, generally; sometimes, longer, if the business requires it. If the business is very long, or likely to be very long, an adjournment takes place at four o'clock, and the court sits the following day. On many occasions, I have had to sit for upwards of a week together in insolvency.
periodthree 31. Are those hours strictly kept? Well; pretty strictly kept. Yes. Sometimes, especially in term time, the Chief Justice and I have to confer before we go into court on some point that has arisen on the previous day, or on some matters of practice; and, as we see very little of one another, except during term time, that is a very convenient time to dispose of any points of law, or matters of practice, that may have arisen.
periodthree 127. Do you think that the business of the Supreme Court is such, that the time has arrived for the appointment of a third judge? No, I do not. Whenever the judges find that they cannot do their work, they will make application to the Executive for assistance.
periodthree 128. Do you not think it would be more satisfactory to litigants that there should be a third judge sitting in cases of appeal, or three judges? No; I do not, as matters stand. Prima facie, it may seem objectionable that one judge, the Chief Justice - who, after all, is only primus inter pares - should have a double vote; but in practice, the regulation has worked well. We have very rarely differed in opinion - very rarely indeed; and when we have differed - perhaps not half-a-dozen times in half-a-dozen years that we have sat together - it has been upon points of minor importance.
periodthree 129. Are appeals against judgments in Queensland as frequent as in New South Wales? We have never had an appeal since the Supreme Court was instituted.

periodthree 4. Do you consider yourself the father of the Bar, here? Yes, I am the oldest practitioner in this colony of longer standing at the Bar than anyone in this colony.
periodthree 5. Have you reason to think, Mr. Blake, that the appointment of a third Judge of the Supreme Court would be of advantage to the colony? I think it would be a decided advantage. Indeed, I think that, for the administration of justice, and the proper administration of the law, it is essential. I can give you my reasons.
periodthree 6. Will you state your reasons, if you please, why you have come to that conclusion? Because, in the first place, there is no tribunal composed of two judges [as the Queensland Supreme Court then was], even if they were men of considerable ability and legal knowledge, that is not an imperfect tribunal. There is a great difficulty in two men, constantly sitting together, coming to an independent conclusion; they generally try, if they differ in opinion - they must constantly try - to accommodate matters between them, each giving up a portion. Whereas, if there are three, each forms a distinct and an independent opinion, and the majority decides: in fact, when I say three, it is an odd number. In England and Ireland, the feeling of the profession is opposed to two judges, though there are two in the Courts of Lords Justices of Appeal in Chancery; but they are not open to the same objection, because they are strictly Courts of Appeal; and there is a judge of the court below - there is the opinion of the judge below - so there are, in effect, three; if they differ, one must coincide with the judge of the court below. But I find that, even there, they are objected to. In the recent report of the Commission - published the other day to investigate the law system in England, I find that one of the recommendations is, that no court consisting of more than one judge should consist of less than three. That commission has the ablest men in England on it.
periodthree 7. Are you not aware that the Chief Justice has the power of giving the casting vote? I am. I think that a very injudicious power - I believe that it is. I do not know of its ever having been exercised. I think the present Chief Justice is about the last man in the world to exercise it.
periodthree 8. Then, truly, if they differ now, one has to accommodate himself to the other? That is the course. From my experience, that is what is done.
periodthree 9. Can you give any other reason? I can give you a remarkable instance of that which occurred recently; in the case that was tried at Rockhampton, McGavin and Mac Master. In that case, the Chief Justice ruled upon a very nice legal question, wrongly, according to my opinion; and the verdict of the jury was clearly against the weight of evidence; and the matter was brought before the court for a new trial. Mr. Justice Lutwyche appeared to be of a different opinion from the Chief Justice; and, ultimately, they decided the case in the singular way, that they affirmed the ruling of the Chief Justice, but granted a new trial, because the verdict was against evidence; and they made the plaintiff pay the costs of the former trial, or directed him to pay the costs of the former trial; but the plaintiff, from his inability to pay those costs, has been unable to proceed any further. Now, if there had been three judges, the record of that case would have been entirely different, in my opinion.
periodthree 10. Do you think the public is inconvenienced, seriously, by delays consequent upon there not being a third judge? I do. I think the unsatisfactory way in which the law business is done must be very prejudicial to the country - - must be very injurious; in fact, I know people suffer a great deal from it. [208]
periodthree 11. Do you find, at times, that cases in which you are interested are seriously retarded, for want of your being able to obtain the attention of a judge? I cannot say they are retarded, in consequence of there not being a third judge. I think that they would be much more satisfactorily determined if there were a third judge. I think they are more retarded from the way in which the business of the court is managed.
periodthree 12. Will you explain, further what you mean by the business being retarded? - In consequence of the way in which the rules are managed? Well, the principal objection is this: the business of the year is compressed into small periods, and then there are large intervals when, in fact, there is nothing doing.
periodthree 13. Those intervals are called vacations? No: there are only, strictly, two vacations in the year. I have got the paper of the court before me, which I shall call your attention to: - the Christmas vacation commenced on Saturday, the 19th of December, 1868, and ended on Saturday, 13th February, 1869. Winter vacation commenced on Saturday, 5th June; ended on Saturday, 10th July, 1869. These are the vacations, strictly so called. I think the winter vacations unnecessarily and needlessly long. I do not think the summer is, for it is essential to everybody: it is not so long as in England - it is two months, summer vacation. It is essential for the people in this country, to enable them to get a rest, after the year's work; - a shorter vacation than that would not allow the members of the profession to take some recreation, which they all do. At that hot season of the year, I do not think that is too long. The winter vacation is. But it will be necessary to look over - 
periodthree 14. May I ask you one question, before you go further? - Do you think it is absolutely necessary that there should be vacations? Oh! yes; I think so. I think there should be a summer vacation of not less than six weeks. During that time, of course, one judge would - as they do in New South Wales, as everywhere - attend to whatever business might arise. Of course, if there were three judges, the other two - as in New South Wales, or as in England, all but one - can go anywhere they please. One judge always remains at home - they take it alternately - to transact whatever business may arise during that time.
periodthree 15. You were continuing your statement when I interrupted you? I was saying that the business is compressed into too short periods of time to allow it to be got through. There are four sittings in Brisbane for the trial of causes, in the year, for each of which the judges allow only a week, and, the week before term; so that there is no opportunity given to extend the sittings, if necessary.
periodthree 16. And, if the business is not done during that week, what is the result? Such as what has taken place, recently, on three or four occasions; - that the business has to be postponed and heard at such intervals of time as can be obtained from other business.
periodthree 17. Do those postponements add to the expenses of the litigants? Enormously. The principal expense is witnesses - retaining witnesses, who have, on many occasions, to be kept during all this time, and other expenses; of course, every expense is increased by it, but the great expense is in witnesses.
